cues.text: Forty Hours on a French Island
On January 26, 1902, at the parish church of Saint-Andre on the French island of La Reunion in the Indian Ocean, Father Henry Lacombe was celebrating the Forty Hours devotion.
The parish's pastor had the Blessed Sacrament exposed in the monstrance on the altar.
As he began the Mass and reached the elevation, his own account records that he lifted his eyes toward the Host and saw a bright halo surrounding the rays of the monstrance.
A Priest's Own Account
Father Lacombe later described his own reaction to what he saw.
He continued reciting the prayers of the Mass, he wrote, “with great agitation in my soul but which I tried to overcome.”
According to his own testimony and that of the growing crowd around him, what had begun as an unusual light around the monstrance soon resolved.
It became a clear and detailed image of the face of Jesus within the Host itself.
A Crowd, and a Sketch

As word spread through the town, the whole population of Saint-Andre made its way to the church to see what was happening, joined before long by journalists and visitors from the island's capital, Saint-Denis.

Father Lacombe took precautions against natural explanations, extinguishing the candles and closing the shutters to rule out any trick of reflected light — the image, he reported, only grew clearer in the resulting darkness.
A young artist among the crowd sketched the face as it appeared, and the vision later changed again to show a crucifix covering the entire Host before fading following the Eucharistic blessing.
Recounted at a Eucharistic Congress
Father Lacombe himself later recounted the event publicly on more than one occasion — to thousands gathered at the Eucharistic Congress of Angouleme in 1904 and to priests at a retreat in Perigueux.
This gives the account an unusually direct paper trail: not a later retelling by others, but the celebrant's own repeated, first-person testimony delivered within a few years of the event itself.
Legacy
The Saint-Andre account stands out among twentieth-century Eucharistic traditions for resting so directly on the sworn word of the priest closest to it.
He described his inner struggle to keep celebrating Mass while watching something he could not explain unfold above the altar where he stood.

What the congregation of Saint-Andre carried away that January morning was not simply a report passed down through others, but the testimony of their own pastor, given in his own words, of what he had seen with his own eyes.
